description: Graduate algorithm design and analysis: amortisation, randomisation, approximation, linear programming, online and streaming models, parameterised algorithms and lower bounds. Students prove guarantees on paper and then step through, implement and measure each algorithm in the lab, finishing with a research-paper reproduction project.
modelledOn: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms
Williamson and Shmoys, The Design of Approximation Algorithms
outcomes: Analyse data structures with aggregate, accounting and potential arguments and justify their amortised bounds.
Design randomised algorithms and bound their error and running time using Markov, Chebyshev and Chernoff inequalities.
Construct approximation algorithms with proven ratios using greedy, rounding and primal-dual techniques.
Formulate problems as linear programs, derive duals and use duality to certify optimality or design algorithms.
Evaluate online and streaming algorithms by competitive ratio and space bounds, and analyse FPT and exact exponential algorithms.
Read, reproduce and critique a research paper on algorithms with a short written report.

units.title: Amortised analysis and advanced data structures
topics: Aggregate, accounting and potential methods of amortised analysis
Dynamic arrays, binary counters and splay trees
Fibonacci heaps, decrease-key and the faster Dijkstra and Prim algorithms
Union-find with path compression and union by rank; the inverse Ackermann bound
Persistent data structures and van Emde Boas trees

units.title: Randomised algorithms and probabilistic analysis
topics: Probability tools: linearity of expectation, Markov, Chebyshev and Chernoff-type bounds
Las Vegas and Monte Carlo algorithms; randomised quicksort and selection
Random contraction algorithm for minimum cut and success amplification
Universal, perfect and cuckoo hashing
Randomised primality testing (strong pseudoprime test) and polynomial identity testing
Derandomisation by the method of conditional expectations

units.title: Approximation algorithms
topics: Approximation ratio, PTAS and FPTAS; the 2-approximation for vertex cover
Greedy set cover with its logarithmic ratio; metric TSP: doubling tree and Christofides
Dynamic programming and rounding: the knapsack FPTAS
LP rounding and primal-dual: weighted vertex cover and facility location
Semidefinite relaxations: hyperplane rounding for max-cut; hardness of approximation and the PCP theorem

units.title: Linear programming and duality
topics: Linear program formulations, geometry of polytopes and the simplex method
Weak and strong duality, complementary slackness and Farkas' lemma
Max-flow min-cut and bipartite matching as LPs; total unimodularity
Ellipsoid and interior-point methods overview; integer programming and branch and bound
The multiplicative weights update method and its applications

units.title: Online and streaming algorithms
topics: Competitive analysis: ski rental and paging with the k-competitive bound for LRU
Randomised online algorithms and list update
Streaming model: reservoir sampling and frequent-items summaries heavy hitters
Count-min sketch, count sketch and HyperLogLog for distinct counts
MinHash and k-mer sketches for comparing genomes

units.title: Parameterised and exact exponential algorithms
topics: Fixed-parameter tractability: kernelisation and bounded search trees for vertex cover
Treewidth and dynamic programming on tree decompositions
Colour coding, the W-hierarchy and parameterised hardness
Exact exponential algorithms: subset dynamic programming, inclusion-exclusion and meet in the middle
SAT algorithms: DPLL, random-walk and the exponential time hypothesis

units.title: Lower bounds and the limits of computation
topics: Decision-tree lower bounds and adversary arguments
NP-completeness, reductions, co-NP and the polynomial hierarchy at a glance
The minimax principle and lower bounds for randomised algorithms
Communication complexity and lower bounds for streaming
Fine-grained complexity: 3SUM, all-pairs shortest paths and SETH-based hardness

units.title: Research project
topics: Critical reading of an algorithms paper: claims, proof sketch and assumptions
Implementation and empirical evaluation methodology for algorithms
Survey of open problems and how to frame a result
Project presentation and peer review

schedule.title: Amortised analysis
schedule.exercise: Prove an amortised O(1) bound for increment on a binary counter with each of the three methods, and analyse a dynamic array that grows by doubling versus adding a constant.

tasks.title: Step through 16 increments of a binary counter, record actual and amortised costs per step, and check the totals against the accounting argument
Implement a dynamic array with doubling and with fixed-size growth, count element copies over one million appends, and plot the average cost per append
Run a sequence of splay tree accesses, track the potential function after each splay, and verify the amortised bound for a skewed access pattern

schedule.title: Heaps, union-find and persistence
schedule.exercise: Show why decrease-key is cheap in a Fibonacci heap, and trace union-find with path compression on a sequence of unions and finds.

tasks.title: Trace union-find with union by rank and path compression through 12 operations and draw the forest after each union
Implement Dijkstra with a binary heap and with a Fibonacci heap on random graphs, and compare operation counts as edges grow
Build a persistent balanced tree using path copying, query three past versions, and measure memory per update against an in-place tree

schedule.title: Probabilistic tools and basic randomised algorithms
schedule.exercise: Bound the failure probability of repeating the random contraction algorithm n squared times, and prove the expected comparison count of randomised quicksort.

tasks.title: Run randomised quicksort and quickselect on 10 inputs with chosen pivots and count comparisons against the expected 2n ln n bound
Simulate 10,000 sums of independent coin flips, plot the tail, and compare it with the Markov, Chebyshev and Chernoff-type bounds
Implement random contraction, run it repeatedly on a given graph, and plot the success probability against the number of repetitions and the theoretical bound

schedule.title: Hashing and randomised testing
schedule.exercise: Show that a universal hash family gives expected constant lookup time, and run the strong pseudoprime test test on a Carmichael number.

tasks.title: Insert 20 keys into a cuckoo hash table, trace the displacement chains, and note when a rehash is triggered
Implement strong pseudoprime test, test it on 50 primes and 50 composites including Carmichael numbers, and report the observed error rate against the 4 to the minus k bound
Derandomise the random-cut 1/2-approximation for max-cut using conditional expectations, and compare the cut with the randomised result on 10 graphs

schedule.title: Basic approximation algorithms
schedule.exercise: Prove the 2-approximation for vertex cover and the doubling-tree bound for metric TSP, and build the knapsack FPTAS for a given epsilon.

tasks.title: Run the maximal-matching vertex cover on five graphs, compare each cover with the optimum found by brute force, and check the ratio never exceeds 2
Implement greedy set cover and the doubling-tree TSP tour on random instances and compare their cost with optimal values from a small exact solver
Implement the knapsack FPTAS, run it for epsilon 0.5, 0.1 and 0.01 on a fixed instance, and plot solution quality against running time

schedule.title: LP rounding, primal-dual and hardness
schedule.exercise: Round the LP relaxation of weighted vertex cover to a 2-approximation, and sketch the semidefinite hyperplane rounding argument.

tasks.title: Solve the LP relaxation of weighted vertex cover on a small graph, round at one half, and compare the cost with the optimal integer cover
Implement the primal-dual algorithm for facility location, run it on a 20-site instance, and verify the dual feasibility and the cost bound
Implement hyperplane rounding for max-cut from a given vector solution, repeat it 1,000 times, and compare the best and average cut with the 0.878 guarantee

schedule.title: Linear programs and duality
schedule.exercise: Formulate a diet or transport LP, take its dual, and use complementary slackness to confirm that a proposed solution is optimal.

tasks.title: Plot the feasible region of a two-variable LP, move the objective line to find the optimum, and trace the simplex path through the vertices
Write the dual of a given LP, solve both, and check strong duality and complementary slackness on the optimal pair
Formulate max-flow and bipartite matching as LPs, solve them, and confirm the solutions are integral and equal the min-cut value

schedule.title: Integer programming and multiplicative weights
schedule.exercise: Compare the LP bound with the integer optimum on a small knapsack by branch and bound, and run multiplicative weights on a zero-sum game.

tasks.title: Step through branch and bound on a knapsack of eight items, showing the LP bound at each node and which branches are pruned
Run multiplicative weights on a 3x3 zero-sum game, plot average regret per round, and compare the value with the LP solution
Solve an LP and its integer version for a facility problem and measure the integrality gap as the instance size is increased

schedule.title: Online and streaming algorithms
schedule.exercise: Prove that LRU is k-competitive, derive the ski-rental ratio, and analyse reservoir sampling and a count-min sketch error bound.

tasks.title: Run LRU, FIFO and an optimal offline policy on 5 request sequences, compute each competitive ratio, and find an adversarial sequence for LRU
Implement reservoir sampling and frequent-items summaries on a stream of 100,000 items and compare the estimated heavy hitters with exact counts
Implement MinHash on k-mers of five short genomes, estimate pairwise Jaccard similarity, and check the error against exact values for 3 sketch sizes

schedule.title: Fixed-parameter tractability
schedule.exercise: Give a kernel for vertex cover with size at most k squared, and write the dynamic programme for maximum independent set on a path decomposition.

tasks.title: Step through a bounded search tree for vertex cover with k equal to 4, showing the branching and the number of nodes visited
Implement dynamic programming for independent set on a tree decomposition of width 3 and verify against brute force on 10 graphs
Implement colour coding to find a simple path of length k, and measure the number of random colourings needed for 95 percent success

schedule.title: Exact exponential algorithms and SAT
schedule.exercise: Compare running times of subset dynamic programming, brute force and meet in the middle for TSP and subset sum, and trace DPLL on a small formula.

tasks.title: Implement subset dynamic programming for TSP and brute force, time both for 8 to 16 cities, and plot growth against n squared times 2 to the n
Trace DPLL with unit propagation on a 12-clause formula, draw the decision tree, and count the backtracks
Implement the random-walk SAT algorithm, run it on satisfiable 3-SAT instances of growing size, and compare its steps with the 4/3 to the n bound

schedule.title: Lower bounds and the limits of computation
schedule.exercise: Prove the n log n comparison bound, a minimax-principle bound for randomised algorithms, and a 3SUM-hardness reduction, and critique a hardness claim.

tasks.title: Draw the decision tree for sorting 4 elements, count its leaves, and play the adversary to force the worst-case number of comparisons
Reduce 3-SAT to independent set for three formulas, build the graphs, and check satisfiability matches the existence of an independent set of size m
Implement the quadratic 3SUM algorithm, test it on 1,000 random lists, and reduce a geometric collinearity check to 3SUM on a small input

schedule.title: Research project
schedule.exercise: Reproduce the main experiment of a chosen algorithms paper, write a two-page critique, and present your results with limitations and open questions.

tasks.title: Read the claims of a paper in a guided case, mark which are proved and which are only empirical, and be scored against a critique rubric
Implement the paper's algorithm and a baseline, run both on 5 input families with fixed seeds, and plot running time with confidence intervals
Find an input that makes your implementation violate a claimed bound or confirm it, and explain the result in the visualiser trace
